newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Wage protests patchy during Yeltsin operation.
newsitem.headline: Wage protests patchy during Yeltsin operation.

text.p: Workers demonstrated across Russia on Tuesday, asking ailing President Boris Yeltsin to pay trillions of roubles (billions of dollars) in wage arrears.
But the patchy protests were far below the mass meetings unions had promised when they called their day of action.
Mining unions said 250 of Russia's 280 mines were closed for the day. Coal company Rosugol, however, said strikes affected only 152 of its 243 mines.

In Moscow journalists estimated that only 5,000-8,000 protesters met in Red Square, less than one-10th of what unions had forecast. About 8,000 gathered in St Petersburg, a local television station said.
A reporter in Yekaterinburg, close to where Europe and Asia meet said just 800 demonstrated in the city centre.
"A sick country needs a healthy president," said defence sector workers calling for new presidential elections in Novosibirsk, a city of 1.5 million people a third of the way across Siberia.
Yeltsin, 65, underwent heart bypass surgery on Tuesday and doctors said the operation had been a success.
The wave of demonstrations began in the port city of Vladivostok, seven time zones east of Moscow, where merchant seaman blew their ships' horns and 20,000 workers massed in the main square.

Union leaders said 160,000 protesters attended meetings in thinly-populated, eastern Primorsky Krai, one region where wage arrears have been particularly acute, but which nevertheless supported Yeltsin during the presidential election in July.
Wage arrears are one of Russia's most pressing economic problems and millions of workers go for months on end without any pay at all.

The head of a once top-secret nuclear research centre in the Urals committed suicide last month, apparently after losing hope of keeping his institution afloat. Workers there had not been paid since May.
Official statistics for late September say workers are owed over 40 trillion roubles ($7.3 billion) by the government and by companies.
The government blames companies which do not pay their taxes. The firms say they are not being paid for goods they supply, often to the impoverished, inefficient defence sector.
In Moscow some demonstrators outside the White House government building said they had not been paid since August.
"We are not interested in the old ways," said 56-year-old Lidiya Kazarnovskaya, from a local engineering research institute. "Don't give us bread -- just give us our pay on which we can live."
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin told the crowd of several hundred that firms had to pay their taxes for the government to pay its debts.
"What's the good if people are not paid their wages?" he said, telling protesters he had signed an order to pay some of the arrears on Tuesday, as soon as government finances allowed.

Mikhail Shmakov, chairman of the national Federation of Independent Trade Unions, welcomed Chernomyrdin's order but said the whole arrears had to be paid. Union leaders will meet on December 5 to plan further action if wages remain unpaid.
